```{python}
#| label: setup
import sys, warnings
sys.path.insert(0, "../slides")
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")
from plotstyle import setup, C
plt = setup()

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

b    = pd.read_parquet("../data/spine/angle_b_sector.parquet")
core = pd.read_parquet("../data/spine/core.parquet")
df   = b.merge(core[["geo", "time", "gdp_pc_eur", "productivity_idx"]], on=["geo", "time"])

BARE = "np.log(annual_earnings_eur) ~ tertiary_share + vacancy_rate + C(nace_r2)"
CTRL = BARE + " + np.log(gdp_pc_eur)"

m  = smf.ols(BARE, data=df).fit()
m2 = smf.ols(CTRL, data=df).fit()
g  = df.loc[m.model.data.row_labels, "geo"]
g2 = df.loc[m2.model.data.row_labels, "geo"]

def parts(fit, groups, name):
    i  = list(fit.params.index).index(name)
    cl = fit.get_robustcov_results(cov_type="cluster", groups=groups)
    hc = fit.get_robustcov_results(cov_type="HC1")
    return (float(np.asarray(fit.bse)[i]), float(np.asarray(hc.bse)[i]),
            float(np.asarray(cl.bse)[i]), float(fit.params.iloc[i]))

cls, hcs, clu, coef = parts(m, g, "tertiary_share")
cls2, _, clu2, coef2 = parts(m2, g2, "tertiary_share")
```

# {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

::: {style="margin-top: 1.2em"}
### Your coefficient has a standard error. When does it mean anything? {style="color:#F7F6F3"}
:::

## Outline

| | |
|---|---|
| **1** | Where we are, and what this adds |
| **2** | The sampling distribution of $\hat\beta$ |

## Learning objectives

::: {.tight}
- Decompose $\hat\beta$ into truth plus noise, and see what each assumption buys
- Read the **four levers** in the variance of a single coefficient
- State **Gauss–Markov** and say precisely where it stops applying
- Compute classical, **HC1** and **cluster-robust** standard errors, and choose between them
- **Sign an omitted-variable bias before estimating**, then check the prediction
:::

# 1 · What this adds {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## Session 02 gave you a number

You can now fit a line and say exactly what it optimises.

::: {.warn}
What you cannot yet say is whether that number would survive a different sample — and therefore
whether it means anything at all.
:::

## What today adds

| Session 02 | Session 03 |
|---|---|
| $\hat\beta$ | a standard error that is actually correct |
| The projection | the *sampling distribution* of the projection |
| "Controlling for" as geometry | what happens when you control for the **wrong** things |
| One dataset | the thought experiment of many datasets |

::: {.check}
Session 02 was deterministic linear algebra. **Session 03 is where randomness enters** — and almost
everything that goes wrong in applied work goes wrong here.
:::

# 2 · The sampling distribution {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## The decomposition that is all of inference

Substitute $y = X\beta + \varepsilon$ into $\hat\beta = (X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top y$:

$$\hat\beta = \beta + (X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top\varepsilon$$

::: {.check}
Truth, plus a term that is pure noise. Everything that follows depends **only** on what you are
willing to assume about $\varepsilon$.
:::

## Unbiasedness is cheap

$$\mathbb{E}[\hat\beta \mid X] = \beta + (X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon\mid X] = \beta$$

using only **strict exogeneity**.

::: {.muted}
Note what is *not* needed: no homoskedasticity, no normality, no independence. Unbiasedness is a
weak requirement — which is why it is a weak reassurance.
:::

## The variance, and its four levers

Under homoskedasticity, for one coefficient:

$$\mathrm{Var}(\hat\beta_j) = \frac{\sigma^2}{n \cdot \mathrm{Var}(x_j) \cdot (1 - R_j^2)}$$

::: {.tight}
- $\sigma^2$ — **noise** you cannot reduce
- $n$ — **sample size**
- $\mathrm{Var}(x_j)$ — **variation in the regressor**: no variation, no estimate
- $1/(1-R_j^2)$ — **redundancy**, the variance inflation factor
:::

## What redundancy costs

```{python}
r2 = np.linspace(0, 0.985, 300)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 2.8))
ax.plot(r2, 1 / (1 - r2), color=C.accent, lw=2.4)
for v, lab in [(5, "VIF 5 — worth a comment"), (10, "VIF 10 — barely identified")]:
    ax.axhline(v, color=C.warn, ls=":", lw=1.2)
    ax.text(0.02, v + 1.8, lab, color=C.warn, fontsize=8.5)
ax.set_xlabel(r"$R_j^2$ — how well the other regressors explain $x_j$")
ax.set_ylabel("variance inflation factor"); ax.set_ylim(0, 45)
plt.show()
```

::: {.check}
This is the price of collinearity — and exactly what regularisation in Session 05 proposes to pay
**differently**.
:::

# 3 · Gauss–Markov {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## The theorem

> Under assumptions 1–4, $\hat\beta_{OLS}$ has the **smallest variance among linear unbiased
> estimators**.

*Sketch.* Any linear unbiased $\tilde\beta = Cy$ has $C = (X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top + D$ with $DX = 0$;
then $\mathrm{Var}(\tilde\beta) = \sigma^2[(X^\top X)^{-1} + DD^\top] \succeq \mathrm{Var}(\hat\beta)$.
$\blacksquare$

## Read the middle word

**B**est **L**inear **U**nbiased **E**stimator.

::: {.warn}
The guarantee holds only **within the class of unbiased estimators**. Sessions 04 and 05 show that
accepting bias deliberately can lower total error. Gauss–Markov does not forbid that — it simply
does not apply.
:::

# 4 · When assumption 4 fails {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## Look at the residuals first

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.scatter(m.fittedvalues, m.resid, s=9, color=C.accent, alpha=.35, edgecolor="none")
ax.axhline(0, color=C.muted, lw=1.2)
ax.set_xlabel("fitted values"); ax.set_ylabel("residual")
ax.set_title("earnings model — is the spread constant?")
plt.show()
```

::: {.check}
You are looking for a **shape**, not running a test. In this panel the error variance scales with
country size.
:::

## The sandwich is always correct

$$\mathrm{Var}(\hat\beta\mid X) = (X^\top X)^{-1}\big(X^\top \Omega X\big)(X^\top X)^{-1},
\qquad \Omega = \mathrm{Var}(\varepsilon\mid X)$$

| Guess at $\Omega$ | When |
|---|---|
| $\sigma^2 I$ — classical | essentially never with a real panel |
| $\mathrm{diag}(\hat\varepsilon_i^2)$ — **HC1** | variance differs across units |
| $\sum_g \hat\varepsilon_g\hat\varepsilon_g^\top$ — **cluster** | errors correlated within a unit |

::: {.check}
$\hat\beta$ never changes. Only your claimed **precision** does.
:::

# 5 · Three standard errors {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## The same coefficient, three intervals

```{python}
labels = ["classical", "HC1", "cluster by country"]
ses    = [cls, hcs, clu]
cols   = [C.muted, C.accent, C.warn]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.8, 2.5))
for i, (lab, s, col) in enumerate(zip(labels, ses, cols)):
    ax.errorbar(coef, i, xerr=1.96 * s, fmt="o", color=col, capsize=5, lw=2.4, ms=7)
    ax.text(coef + 1.96 * s + .012, i, f"±{1.96*s:.3f}", color=col, va="center", fontsize=9)
ax.axvline(0, color=C.ink, ls=":", lw=1.2)
ax.set_yticks(range(3)); ax.set_yticklabels(labels)
ax.set_xlabel("coefficient on tertiary_share, with 95% interval")
ax.set_ylim(-.6, 2.6); ax.grid(axis="y", alpha=0)
plt.show()
```

```{python}
print(f"  classical {cls:.4f}    HC1 {hcs:.4f}    cluster {clu:.4f}"
      f"    →  cluster/classical = {clu/cls:.2f}x")
```

::: {.warn}
The clustered interval is about **3× wider**. A $t$-statistic of 6 was really a $t$ of 2.
:::

## Now watch it disappear

Add one country-level control — $\log$ GDP per capita:

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.8, 2.4))
pairs = [("without GDP control", cls, clu, coef), ("with GDP control", cls2, clu2, coef2)]
for i, (lab, sc, sk, cf) in enumerate(pairs):
    ax.errorbar(cf, i + .13, xerr=1.96 * sc, fmt="o", color=C.muted, capsize=4, lw=2)
    ax.errorbar(cf, i - .13, xerr=1.96 * sk, fmt="o", color=C.warn, capsize=4, lw=2)
    ax.text(cf + 1.96 * max(sc, sk) + .015, i, f"ratio {sk/sc:.2f}x",
            color=C.ink, va="center", fontsize=9.5, fontweight="600")
ax.set_yticks([0, 1]); ax.set_yticklabels([p[0] for p in pairs])
ax.set_title("grey = classical      red = clustered", fontsize=9)
ax.set_xlabel("coefficient on tertiary_share")
ax.set_ylim(-.7, 1.7); ax.grid(axis="y", alpha=0)
plt.show()
```

## Why it disappeared

$\log(\text{GDP per capita})$ varies at the **country-year** level, so including it **absorbs the
common shock** that was making residuals correlate within a country.

::: {.tight}
- Clustering matters when a **shared, unmodelled** shock sits in the residual
- Model that shock explicitly and the correction shrinks
- Neither route is cheating — the same fact, handled in two places
:::

::: {.warn}
Do **not** conclude "clustering never matters, just add controls". A control that absorbs the shock
may also absorb the variation you wanted to study.
:::

## Which one do you report?

::: {.tight}
- Cluster **at the level at which treatment varies** and shocks are shared — here, `geo`
- Report the number of **clusters** alongside $n$: 3,150 rows, **30 countries**
- Below roughly **40 clusters**, cluster-robust inference is itself unreliable
:::

::: {.warn}
"Robust standard errors" in a table note, with no cluster level named, tells the reader nothing.
:::

# 6 · Omitted variable bias {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## The formula

True model $y = X_1\beta_1 + X_2\beta_2 + u$, estimated on $X_1$ alone. With $\delta$ from
regressing $X_2$ on $X_1$:

$$\mathbb{E}[\hat\beta_1] = \beta_1 + \delta\beta_2$$

## Sign it with two questions

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 2.3))
ax.axis("off")
cells = [(r"$\delta>0,\ \beta_2>0$", "upward", C.warn),
         (r"$\delta<0,\ \beta_2<0$", "upward", C.warn),
         (r"$\delta>0,\ \beta_2<0$", "downward", C.good),
         (r"$\delta<0,\ \beta_2>0$", "downward", C.good)]
for i, (cond, direction, col) in enumerate(cells):
    x  = .04 + (i % 2) * .50
    yy = .66 - (i // 2) * .45
    ax.text(x, yy, cond, fontsize=11.5, color=C.ink)
    ax.annotate("", xy=(x + .29, yy + (.06 if direction == "upward" else -.06)),
                xytext=(x + .23, yy), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=col, lw=2.6))
    ax.text(x + .32, yy, direction, fontsize=10.5, color=col, fontweight="600")
plt.show()
```

::: {.check}
**Same sign in both → upward bias.** Answer both questions in writing *before* estimating. It costs
nothing, and it is the most useful discipline in applied work.
:::

## Then test the prediction

```{python}
short = smf.ols("np.log(annual_earnings_eur) ~ tertiary_share", data=df).fit()
lng   = smf.ols("np.log(annual_earnings_eur) ~ tertiary_share + productivity_idx", data=df).fit()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.2, 2.1))
ax.barh([1], [short.params["tertiary_share"]], color=C.warn, height=.45)
ax.barh([0], [lng.params["tertiary_share"]], color=C.good, height=.45)
ax.set_yticks([0, 1]); ax.set_yticklabels(["with productivity", "omitting productivity"])
for yy, v in [(1, short.params["tertiary_share"]), (0, lng.params["tertiary_share"])]:
    ax.text(v + .03, yy, f"{v:.3f}", va="center", fontsize=10.5, fontweight="600", color=C.ink)
ax.set_xlabel("coefficient on tertiary_share"); ax.grid(axis="y", alpha=0)
plt.show()
```

::: {.check}
Productive countries have higher earnings ($\beta_2>0$) **and** higher tertiary shares
($\delta>0$), so the bias should be **upward** — the short coefficient should exceed the long one.
It does.
:::

# 7 · What it identifies {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## The Mincer example

$$\log w_i = \alpha + \rho S_i + \gamma_1 X_i + \gamma_2 X_i^2 + \varepsilon_i$$

$\rho$ is often read as "the return to a year of schooling". Strictly, it is

> the mean log-wage difference associated with an additional year of schooling **among people
> otherwise identical on the included covariates.**

::: {.warn}
Unobserved ability, selection into schooling and measurement error each break the causal reading.
Session 10 supplies tools that take this seriously.
:::

::: {.check}
Today the discipline is simply to **say precisely what you have estimated.**
:::

# 8 · Key takeaways {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## What to carry out of this session

::: {.tight}
1. $\hat\beta = \beta + (X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top\varepsilon$ — **everything follows from the second term**
2. Unbiasedness is cheap; **precision is where the assumptions bite**
3. The sandwich is always right; classical, HC1 and cluster are three guesses at $\Omega$
4. **Cluster where treatment varies**, name the level, report the cluster count
5. **Sign the omitted-variable bias before estimating**, then check
6. A $p$-value answers "how surprising under the null" — not "how large", not "is the model right"
:::

## What loses marks reliably

| | |
|---|---|
| Default standard errors on panel data | intervals far too narrow |
| "Robust SEs" with no cluster level named | unreproducible |
| Reading significance off $n=3{,}150$ | you have 30 independent units |
| Controlling for everything | post-treatment bias; uninterpretable coefficients |
| A $p$-value reported as an effect size | give the magnitude, in units |

## In the practice session

::: {.tight}
1. Fit the specification; inspect residuals against fitted values
2. Compute classical, HC1 and cluster-robust standard errors side by side
3. Name a confounder, **sign its bias**, then test the prediction
4. Report the coefficient with the cluster level and the cluster count
:::
